# Finding the Antiderivative of -3*exp(x)*cos(x)

## Step 1: Factor out the constant
$$\int -3\cdot\exp(x)\cdot\cos(x)\,dx = -3\int \exp(x)\cdot\cos(x)\,dx$$

## Step 2: Compute I = ∫ exp(x)·cos(x) dx via integration by parts

**First integration by parts:** u = cos(x), dv = exp(x)dx → du = -sin(x)dx, v = exp(x)

$$I = \exp(x)\cdot\cos(x) + \int \exp(x)\cdot\sin(x)\,dx$$

**Second integration by parts** on the remaining integral: u = sin(x), dv = exp(x)dx → du = cos(x)dx, v = exp(x)

$$\int \exp(x)\cdot\sin(x)\,dx = \exp(x)\cdot\sin(x) - \int \exp(x)\cdot\cos(x)\,dx = \exp(x)\cdot\sin(x) - I$$

## Step 3: Solve for I

$$I = \exp(x)\cdot\cos(x) + \exp(x)\cdot\sin(x) - I$$
$$2\cdot I = \exp(x)\cdot\cos(x) + \exp(x)\cdot\sin(x)$$
$$I = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\exp(x)\cdot(\cos(x) + \sin(x))$$

## Step 4: Apply the constant multiplier

$$-3 \cdot I = -\frac{3}{2}\cdot\exp(x)\cdot(\cos(x) + \sin(x)) + C$$

## Verification
Differentiating: $-\frac{3}{2}\cdot[\exp(x)\cdot(\cos(x)+\sin(x)) + \exp(x)\cdot(-\sin(x)+\cos(x))]$
$= -\frac{3}{2}\cdot\exp(x)\cdot[2\cos(x)] = -3\cdot\exp(x)\cdot\cos(x)$ ✓

<answer> -3/2*exp(x)*(cos(x) + sin(x)) + C </answer>
